API reference / @jsprismarine/entity-goals

@jsprismarine/entity-goals ​

All 170 vanilla Bedrock minecraft:behavior.* goals, plus the A* path finder they navigate with. It is written against the goal seam of @jsprismarine/entities, which owns the Goal interface, the priority and control_flags parsing and the scheduler; this package owns what each goal does.

typescript
import { EntityTypes } from '@jsprismarine/entities';
import { createGoalEntityRegistry } from '@jsprismarine/entity-goals';

const types = new EntityTypes({ components: createGoalEntityRegistry({ world: (entity) => worlds.get(entity) }) });
const zombie = types.spawn('minecraft:zombie', { environment: { actuator } });

zombie.tick(); // the scheduler runs one goal per control flag

createGoalEntityRegistry registers these goals first and then every non-goal component the entity runtime implements. The order matters: registerEntityComponents skips a name that is already registered, and it ships its own reference versions of float, random_stroll and look_at_player. Calling registerVanillaGoals(registry) on a registry that already holds those three leaves them alone and returns their names.

The goal inventory ​

utils/build-inventory.ts reads the composed vanilla behavior pack and writes src/generated/goalInventory.json: every goal name, how many of the 129 entity files use it, the union of parameter keys observed under it with their JSON types, and which entities carry it. Everything here is written against that file, and src/totality.test.ts fails when a name in it has no registered factory.

Regenerate it with pnpm --filter @jsprismarine/entity-goals run inventory, which needs the sources pnpm --filter @jsprismarine/bedrock-data run fetch:sources caches.

Measured against Bedrock Dedicated Server 1.26.51.1:

MeasureResult
Entity definitions129
Distinct minecraft:behavior.* names170
Names with a registered factory170
Entities whose every goal is implemented129 of 129
Entities that declare at least one goal92
Entities with no goals at all37
Most goals on one entity27 (minecraft:villager_v2)
Goals exactly one entity uses91
Goals at most two entities use123

The twenty most used goals, with how many entity files declare each: look_at_player 69, random_stroll 64, random_look_around 55, float 49, nearest_attackable_target 49, hurt_by_target 42, panic 37, melee_box_attack 32, tempt 31, avoid_mob_type 28, breed 26, mount_pathing 26, follow_parent 24, pickup_items 20, equip_item 17, ranged_attack 14, random_swim 12, player_ride_tamed 10, find_mount 8, flee_sun 7.

Where the values come from ​

Thirty of Java's goal class names match a Bedrock goal name after snake-casing, so for those the constants are read out of the unobfuscated 26.3 server jar rather than guessed, and the JSDoc on the goal names the class. Examples: the 0.02 chance per tick and the 40 to 80 tick hold in look_at_player are LookAtPlayerGoal.DEFAULT_PROBABILITY and its start; the 20-tick swing cadence and 10-tick re-path interval in the melee goals are MeleeAttackGoal; the 2-to-4-block window and 1-in-5 roll in leap_at_target are LeapAtTargetGoal; the 8-block partner search, 60-tick courtship and 3-block distance in breed are BreedGoal; the 300-tick revenge memory in hurt_by_target is HurtByTargetGoal.

Where the two editions disagree the Bedrock parameter wins, because these are Bedrock definitions. Two cases are worth naming. Java's TemptGoal scares the entity off when the player moves more than 0.1 blocks or turns more than 5 degrees; Bedrock spells that as the single can_get_scared flag, which is parsed and handed to the server, because the goal seam carries no player rotation. Java splits melee into one class; Bedrock has melee_attack and melee_box_attack, which differ in whether the reach test uses the distance or the collision boxes, and with no collision boxes in the seam both run the same loop with reach_multiplier as the only difference.

The navigation model ​

findPath is A* over whole blocks against an injected NavigationView. A server implements the view; the first four members are required and the rest are optional, so a goal degrades rather than throwing when the server cannot answer one yet.

typescript
export interface NavigationView {
    blockAt(position: EntityPosition): string | undefined;
    isPassable(position: EntityPosition): boolean;
    isSolid(position: EntityPosition): boolean;
    isWater(position: EntityPosition): boolean;
    isLava(position: EntityPosition): boolean;
    doorAt?(position: EntityPosition): DoorState | undefined;
    isDamaging?(position: EntityPosition): boolean;
    isSunlit?(position: EntityPosition): boolean;
    isPortal?(position: EntityPosition): boolean;
    isClimbable?(position: EntityPosition): boolean;
    isLadder?(position: EntityPosition): boolean;
}

Three media decide which cells a profile may enter, and a cell is enterable when any enabled medium accepts it: ground when the entity stands on something, swim when the cell is a liquid it moves through, and fly when the cell is open air. minecraft:navigation.climb adds vertical moves through climbable blocks, while minecraft:can_climb enables vertical moves through ladder blocks for any navigation type. A ground move keeps its height, steps up one block when the profile jumps, or falls to the first supported cell within the fall limit. Diagonal moves cost sqrt(2) and may not cut a corner.

NavigationProfile comes from the entity's active minecraft:navigation.* component, which @jsprismarine/entities already parses, plus three facts that component does not carry: the height from minecraft:collision_box, the step height from minecraft:variable_max_auto_step, and a fall limit of 3 blocks. The separate minecraft:can_climb marker adds ladder traversal. The flags map onto the search like this.

  • can_pass_doors, can_open_doors, can_open_iron_doors, can_break_doors. An open door needs can_pass_doors. A closed one needs can_open_doors, and an iron one needs can_open_iron_doors as well, or can_break_doors.
  • avoid_water. A water cell costs 8 extra when the profile can float, swim or is amphibious, and is refused otherwise.
  • can_path_over_water, can_path_over_lava, can_walk_in_lava. These decide whether a liquid below the entity carries it, and whether a lava cell may be entered at all.
  • avoid_damage_blocks, avoid_portals, blocks_to_avoid. These refuse a cell outright.
  • avoid_sun. A sunlit cell costs 8 extra rather than being refused, so an entity still paths when there is no shade. flee_sun is the goal that refuses sunlight outright.
  • can_fly, can_swim, can_walk, is_amphibious, can_float. These enable the three media.

The search expands at most 512 nodes unless the caller raises the budget, and returns the closest node it reached only when the request asks for a partial path.

Navigator is the one place that calls the path finder. A goal says where it wants to be and the navigator feeds the actuator one waypoint at a time. With no NavigationView it hands the destination straight to EntityActuator.moveTo and tracks arrival by distance, which is the degraded mode a server gets before it implements the view.

The two seams a server satisfies ​

EntityActuator, from @jsprismarine/entities, is unchanged: position, moveTo, stopMoving, lookAt, jump, randomTarget and nearestPlayer. The goals here use all seven. randomTarget is only consulted when no NavigationView is supplied; with one, the navigator draws candidates and keeps the first the path finder reaches.

GoalWorld is this package's own seam, because the vanilla goals attack, search for blocks, pick up items, mount, trade, breed and teleport, and nothing in EntityActuator reaches any of that. Every member is optional, following the convention FilterEntityView sets: a goal whose world cannot answer what it needs refuses to start. A server supplies one per entity through registerVanillaGoals(registry, { world }).

The members, grouped by what needs them:

  • Sight and surroundings: navigation, mobs, players, items, blocks, canSee, poi, home, setHome.
  • Combat: target, setTarget, damagers, lastPusher, attack, shoot, knockback, push, explode.
  • Items: pickUp, dropItem, giveItem, carriedItem, setCarriedItem, inventory, dropLoot.
  • Blocks and the world: setBlock, breakBlock, spawn, teleportTo, playSound.
  • Relationships: owner, vehicle, riders, mount, dismount, canBreedWith, isReadyToBreed, breedWith, openTrade, tradingPlayer.
  • Flags and reporting: setSitting, setSleeping, trigger, report.

mobs(radius, families) may use the optional family list to narrow a candidate search. It must include every entity in those families; the goal still evaluates the complete data-driven filter before choosing a target.

Everything a filter can already answer is read through EntityInstance.filterContext rather than added here, so the entity's own flags (in_water, is_baby, is_sitting, on_ground and the rest), the time of day and the weather need no new member.

GoalWorld.trigger exists because a goal event with a target other than self has to be routed by the server. An event aimed at self goes through EntityInstance.fire, so its effects land on the entity's next tick like every other event.

Families ​

FileGoalsWhat they share
goals/targeting.ts9Find, hold and release the attack target; no control flags
goals/attacking.ts30Read the target and hurt it; move and look
goals/looking.ts6Turn the head; look only
goals/movement.ts44Wander, swim, fly, flee, follow and walk to a found position
goals/social.ts26Breeding, tempting, owners, mounting, trading and gifts
goals/work.ts14Jobs, farming, item pickup and placing blocks
goals/environment.ts17Sleeping, hiding, sitting and eating a block
goals/specials.ts24The dragon phases and 200-tick death animation, the squid states, the slime and the timer flags

Testing ​

src/harness.ts ships the doubles the package's own tests use, and a server can check its seam implementations against the same ones. RecordingActuator logs every call and moves the entity to whatever it was asked to walk to, voxelGrid builds a NavigationView from layers of text, and GoalHarness puts a real EntityInstance with a real scheduler behind both.

typescript
const harness = new GoalHarness({
    goals: { 'minecraft:behavior.float': { priority: 0, chance_per_tick_to_float: 1 } },
    flags: { in_water: true }
});

harness.tick(3);
harness.holderOf('jump'); // 'minecraft:behavior.float'

src/scheduler.test.ts runs the zombie's nine base goals, with the priorities the vanilla file writes, and shows which goal holds each flag as a player comes into range.

What is left to the server ​

Four things the goals parse and hand over rather than carry out, because the behavior belongs somewhere else.

  • The explosion itself. minecraft:behavior.swell holds the creeper still and the minecraft:explode component does the rest.
  • Villager points of interest. Bedrock has no memory or point-of-interest registry at all, so the work site, the bed, the bell and the village come through GoalWorld.poi and the server decides what counts.
  • Whether two entities may breed. minecraft:breedable owns that rule, so breed and make_love ask GoalWorld.canBreedWith.
  • The ender dragon's flight path. Its eight phase goals are {"priority": n} in the vanilla file and nothing else, so each one holds its phase's control flags for a fixed time and leaves the flight to the server.

minecraft:behavior.avoid_block, which the strider and the hoglin carry. The entity walks away from a block type rather than from a mob.

avoidMobType ​

const avoidMobType: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/movement.ts:565

minecraft:behavior.avoid_mob_type, which 28 vanilla entities carry.

Java's AvoidEntityGoal draws a position 16 blocks out and 7 up away from the threat and refuses it when it is no further from the threat than the entity already is, which is the condition here.

barter ​

const barter: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/social.ts:1079

minecraft:behavior.barter, which the piglin carries. The piglin throws back an item from its barter table once it has finished admiring the gold.

beg ​

const beg: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/social.ts:848

minecraft:behavior.beg, which the wolf carries.

Java's BegGoal holds the beg for 40 to 80 ticks while the player keeps holding an interesting item, which is what look_time spells here.

breed ​

const breed: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/social.ts:76

minecraft:behavior.breed, which 26 vanilla entities carry.

The partner search, the 60-tick courtship and the 3-block distance come from Java's BreedGoal. Whether two entities may breed at all is the server's to answer through GoalWorld.canBreedWith, because the rule lives in minecraft:breedable rather than in the goal.

const defendVillageTarget: RegisterableGoal

Java's DefendVillageTargetGoal scans the golem's own bounding box inflated by its follow range rather than a fixed radius, and prefers a hurt villager's attacker over a raider. This takes the nearest candidate the entity_types table accepts within 64 blocks, because the package has no village model to ask who belongs to it.

Defined in: goals/attacking.ts:203

meleeBoxAttack ​

const meleeBoxAttack: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/attacking.ts:190

minecraft:behavior.melee_box_attack, the attack 32 vanilla entities carry.

Bedrock splits melee in two: this one tests the entity's collision box against the target's, and melee_attack tests the distance. The difference does not survive into a server with no collision boxes in the goal seam, so both run the same loop and reach_multiplier is the only thing that varies.

mingle ​

const mingle: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/social.ts:675

mountPathing ​

const mountPathing: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/movement.ts:1792

minecraft:behavior.mount_pathing, which 26 vanilla entities carry. It is how a mounted entity goes after a target while it is riding something.

Only while it is riding something, which is the gate this goal turns on. The adult zombie carries it at priority 2 and minecraft:behavior. melee_box_attack at priority 4, and both claim the move and look flags, so a version that started on nothing more than having a target took those flags off the attack at every priority below it and left the zombie standing still in front of the player it had chosen. Mojang's own wording is "while mounted", and the vanilla priorities only make sense that way.

tradeInterest ​

const tradeInterest: RegisterableGoal

minecraft:behavior.trade_interest, which the villager and the wandering trader carry. The entity holds up what it would trade when a player comes close carrying something it wants.

tradeWithPlayer ​

const tradeWithPlayer: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/social.ts:980

minecraft:behavior.trade_with_player, which the three trader entities carry.

Java's TradeWithPlayerGoal holds the entity still while the trade screen is open and drops it when the player gets further than 4 blocks away.

transportItems ​

const transportItems: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/work.ts:581

minecraft:behavior.transport_items, which the copper golem carries. It carries items between the containers it can reach.

useKineticWeapon ​

const useKineticWeapon: RegisterableGoal

Defined in: goals/attacking.ts:1398

minecraft:behavior.use_kinetic_weapon, which the five mounted-lance entities carry. The weapon only hurts while its wielder is moving, so the goal rides in, strikes and backs off to build speed again.

Only while the wielder is riding something, which is what the lance is for and what hijack_mount_navigation is about. The zombie, husk, piglin, zombie pigman and zombie villager all carry it on foot as well as mounted, through minecraft:not_on_zombie_horse, and it claims the move and look flags at a priority above minecraft:behavior.melee_box_attack's. A version that started on nothing more than having a target therefore took those flags off the attack and left every zombie that had chosen a player standing still in front of them.

registerVanillaGoals() ​

registerVanillaGoals(registry, options?): readonly string[]

Defined in: register.ts:74

Registers all 170 vanilla minecraft:behavior.* goals with an entity component registry.

A name the registry already carries is left alone, which follows what registerEntityComponents does in @jsprismarine/entities. That matters for three names: minecraft:behavior.float, random_stroll and look_at_player ship there as reference implementations, so register these goals before the components to get this package's versions, or use createGoalEntityRegistry, which does it in that order.

Parameters ​

registry ​

EntityComponentRegistry

The registry the entity types resolve against.

options? ​

VanillaGoalOptions = {}

Returns ​

readonly string[]

The names that were already registered and were left alone.

Example ​

typescript
const types = new EntityTypes({ components: createGoalEntityRegistry({ world }) });
